title: Are You a Passive, Aggressive, or Assertive Teacher?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart Jr. draws on Messages: The Communication Skills Book to present clear behavioral portraits of three teacher communication styles — passive, aggressive, and assertive — and invites teachers to identify which most characterizes their own classroom presence. The passive style is defined by disclaimers, vagueness, physical withdrawal, and the disconnect between what a teacher means and how they come across; the aggressive style by truth-telling at others' expense, humiliation through sarcasm, and an inability to genuinely hear other people; and the assertive style by directness, mutual respect, confident physical bearing, and the capacity to both make and receive difficult communications. Stuart Jr. argues that all three styles are likely present in any teacher's day, but one tends to predominate, and identifying it is a prerequisite for improvement. The piece closes by connecting the assertive style to the research-backed concept of warm-authoritative teacher presence — the stance most associated with student Credibility.
points: Passive teachers signal a lack of conviction through disclaimers, vagueness, and avoiding eye contact — the book's summary: 'Because you are often not saying what you mean, you don't look like you mean what you say.'

Aggressive teachers state their views without regard for others' feelings, tend to humiliate through sarcasm without realizing it, and are so intent on being right that they cannot genuinely hear responses to their own questions.
Assertive teachers make direct statements about their feelings, thoughts, and wishes; stand up for their rights while also honoring others'; and convey assured strength alongside genuine empathy.
All three styles appear in most teachers throughout a school day, but one tends to predominate — identifying that default style is the entry point for deliberate improvement toward assertiveness.

The assertive communication style maps onto what research describes as warm-authoritative teacher presence, making communication style development a direct lever on the Credibility dimension of student motivation.
quotes: Because you are often not saying what you mean, you don't look like you mean what you say.
You are so intent on being right that you don't really hear what others are saying, even when you ask them a direct question.
No problem stating how you feel or what you think, but you tend to state these things at the expense of the feelings and thoughts of others
Tending to humiliate others without knowing it through things like sarcasm and humor

If you're like me, you'll notice that all three styles pop up in you throughout a given school day. Us human beings are complicated! But you'll likely find that one style tends to predominate, and this is something worth reflecting on. The goal is the assertive style, which closely aligns with a warm and authoritative teacher presence.
